entities.name: Quintus Tineius Sacerdos Clemens
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Quintus Tineius Sacerdos Clemens was a prominent Roman senator and religious official who reached the zenith of the Roman political career, the consulship, in 158 CE. As Consul Ordinarius, he held one of the two most prestigious annual magistracies, serving alongside Sextus Sulpicius Tertullus under the reign of Emperor Antoninus Pius. His career trajectory, which also included the esteemed position of Pontifex, illustrates the enduring power and influence of the traditional senatorial aristocracy within the Antonine principate, a period often regarded as the Pax Romana's zenith. His lineage further cemented his family's position, as his son, also named Quintus Tineius Sacerdos, would later achieve the consulship in 219 CE, demonstrating a remarkable continuity of elite status across generations.

His public service likely encompassed a series of magistracies, beginning with the vigintivirate, followed by military tribunate, quaestorship, aedileship or tribunate of the plebs, and praetorship, before culminating in the consulship. These offices were not merely ceremonial but involved concrete administrative and judicial responsibilities, contributing to the governance and infrastructure of the vast Roman Empire. As a Pontifex, Sacerdos Clemens was a member of the most important college of priests in ancient Rome, responsible for maintaining the pax deorum—the peace of the gods—through proper ritual and oversight of religious law, a role critical for state stability and public morale.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Quintus Tineius Sacerdos Clemens represents the stable functioning of the Roman senatorial system during the Antonine period, contributing to the continuity of imperial administration and the perpetuation of the Roman elite. His career exemplifies the social and political mechanisms that maintained the stability of the empire for generations.
